messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor ,
\]

so

\[
m^2\le n\le (m+1)^2-1.
\]

We need

\[
n\mid (m!)^{n!}+450.
\]

We will show that \(n\le 1230\), and then verify that \(n=1230\) works.

---

### 1. Restricting the prime divisors of \(n\)

Let \(p\) be a prime divisor of \(n\). Then \(p\le n\), so \(p-1\mid n!\).

#### Case 1: \(p\le m\)

Then \(p\mid m!\), so

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 0 \pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
(m!)^{n!}+450\equiv 450 \pmod p.
\]

If \(p\mid n\), then \(p\mid (m!)^{n!}+450\), so we must have

\[
p\mid 450.
\]

Since

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,
\]

any prime divisor of \(n\) with \(p\le m\) must be one of \(2,3,5\).

#### Case 2: \(p>m\)

Then \(p\nmid m!\), so \(\gcd(m!,p)=1\). Also \(p-1\mid n!\), so by Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Therefore

\[
(m!)^{n!}+450\equiv 1+450=451 \pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
p\mid 451.
\]

Since

\[
451=11\cdot 41,
\]

any prime divisor of \(n\) with \(p>m\) must be either \(11\) or \(41\).

Also, if \(p>m\), then \(p\ge m+1\), so

\[
p^2\ge (m+1)^2>n.
\]

Hence such a prime can occur to the first power only.

So every prime divisor of \(n\) lies in

\[
\{2,3,5,11,41\}.
\]

---

### 2. Bounding the powers of \(2,3,5\) when \(m\ge 11\)

Suppose \(m\ge 11\). Then \(n\ge m^2\ge 121\), so \(n!\ge 3\).

For each of \(p=2,3,5\), we have \(p\mid m!\), so

\[
p^3\mid (m!)^{n!}.
\]

In particular,

\[
4\mid (m!)^{n!},\qquad 27\mid (m!)^{n!},\qquad 125\mid (m!)^{n!}.
\]

But

\[
4\nmid 450,\qquad 27\nmid 450,\qquad 125\nmid 450.
\]

Therefore

\[
4\nmid (m!)^{n!}+450,\qquad
27\nmid (m!)^{n!}+450,\qquad
125\nmid (m!)^{n!}+450.
\]

Thus, in the prime factorization of \(n\),

\[
v_2(n)\le 1,\qquad v_3(n)\le 2,\qquad v_5(n)\le 2.
\]

---

### 3. Bounding \(m\) and \(n\)

If \(m\le 10\), then

\[
n\le (11)^2-1=120<1230.
\]

Now assume \(m\ge 11\).

If \(m\ge 41\), then both \(11\) and \(41\) are \(\le m\), so neither can divide \(n\). Hence the only possible prime divisors of \(n\) are \(2,3,5\), and from the previous section,

\[
n\le 2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2=450.
\]

But \(m\ge 41\) implies

\[
n\ge m^2\ge 1681,
\]

a contradiction. Therefore

\[
m\le 40.
\]

So the only remaining case is

\[
11\le m\le 40.
\]

In this range, \(11\le m\), so \(11\nmid n\). The only possible large prime factor is \(41\), and it can appear at most once. Thus

\[
n=41^\varepsilon\,2^a3^b5^c
\]

where \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}\), \(0\le a\le 1\), \(0\le b\le 2\), and \(0\le c\le 2\).

Let

\[
S=2^a3^b5^c.
\]

If \(\varepsilon=0\), then

\[
n=S\le 450<1230.
\]

If \(\varepsilon=1\), then \(41\mid n\). Since \(m\le 40\),

\[
n\le (41)^2-1=1680.
\]

Thus

\[
S=\frac n{41}\le \left\lfloor \frac{1680}{41}\right\rfloor=40.
\]

Among all numbers of the form \(2^a3^b5^c\) with \(a\le1\), \(b\le2\), \(c\le2\), the largest one not exceeding \(40\) is \(30\). Therefore

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

So every valid \(n\) satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 4. Verifying that \(n=1230\) works

Let

\[
n=1230.
\]

Then

\[
\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\rfloor =35,
\]

because

\[
35^2=1225\le 1230<1296=36^2.
\]

Also,

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

We check divisibility by \(2\cdot 3\cdot 5=30\) and by \(41\).

Since \(450\mid 35!\), we have

\[
450\mid (35!)^{1230!}.
\]

Also \(450\mid 450\), so

\[
450\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

In particular,

\[
30\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Now consider modulo \(41\). Since \(35<41\), we have \(\gcd(35!,41)=1\). Also \(40\mid 1230!\), so by Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
\]

And

\[
450\equiv -1 \pmod{41}.
\]

Therefore

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1-1\equiv 0 \pmod{41}.
\]

Thus \(41\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450\). Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\),

\[
1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Hence \(n=1230\) is valid, and by the upper bound it is the largest possible.

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
